entries.782e87aa272b8537c2bca1b1982387045b370e28: <div sID="gen19219" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="43" osisID="Ezek.43" sID="Ezek.43"/> <div eID="gen19219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19220" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19221" type="x-p"/> The prophet, having given us a view of the mystical temple, the gospel-church, as he received it from the Lord, that it might appear not to be erected in vain, comes to describe, in this and the next chapter, the worship that should be performed in it, but under the type of the Old-Testament services. In this chapter we have, I. Possession taken of this temple, by the glory of God filling it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.1-Ezek.43.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. A promise given of the continuance of God's presence with his people upon condition of their return to, and continuance in, the instituted way of worship, and their abandoning idols and idolatry, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7-Ezek.43.12">ver. 7-12</reference>. III. A description of the altar of burnt-offerings, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.13-Ezek.43.17">ver. 13-17</reference>. IV. Directions given for the consecration of that altar, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.18-Ezek.43.27">ver. 18-27</reference>. Ezekiel seems here to stand between God and Israel, as Moses the servant of the Lord did when the sanctuary was first set up.
entries.0b14a0de2223b7275ffe957658f36a26a9e6ccaf: <div eID="gen19221" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19220" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Temple. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19222" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Afterward he brought me to the gate, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the gate that looketh toward the east: <hi type="super">2</hi> And, behold, the glory of the God of Israel came from the way of the east: and his voice <hi type="italic">was</hi> like a noise of many waters: and the earth shined with his glory. <hi type="super">3</hi> And <hi type="italic">it was</hi> according to the appearance of the vision which I saw, <hi type="italic">even</hi> according to the vision that I saw when I came to destroy the city: and the visions <hi type="italic">were</hi> like the vision that I saw by the river Chebar; and I fell upon my face. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the glory of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came into the house by the way of the gate whose prospect <hi type="italic">is</hi> toward the east. <hi type="super">5</hi> So the spirit took me up, and brought me into the inner court; and, behold, the glory of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> filled the house. <hi type="super">6</hi> And I heard <hi type="italic">him</hi> speaking unto me out of the house; and the man stood by me. <div eID="gen19222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19223" type="x-p"/> After Ezekiel has patiently surveyed the temple of God, the greatest glory of this earth, he is admitted to a higher form, and honoured with a sight of the glories of the upper world; it is said to him, <hi type="italic">Come up hither.</hi> He has seen the temple, and sees it to be very spacious and splendid; but, till the glory of God comes into it, it is but like the dead bodies he had seen in vision (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.1-Ezek.37.28">ch. xxxvii.</reference>), that had <hi type="italic">no breath</hi> till the Spirit of life entered into them. Here therefore he sees the house filled with God's glory. <div eID="gen19223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19224" type="x-p"/> I. He has a vision of <hi type="italic">the glory of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">the glory of the God of Israel,</hi> that God who is in covenant with Israel, and whom they serve and worship. The idols of the heathen have no glory but what they owe to the goldsmith or the painter; but this is the glory of the God of Israel. This glory <hi type="italic">came from the way of the east,</hi> and therefore he was brought to the <hi type="italic">gate that leads towards the east,</hi> to expect the appearance and approach of it. Christ's <hi type="italic">star was seen in the east,</hi> and he is that <hi type="italic">other angel that ascends out of the east,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.7.2">Rev. vii. 2</reference>. For he is the morning star, he is the sun of righteousness. Two things he observed in this appearance of the glory of God:—1. The power of his word which he heard: <hi type="italic">His voice was like a noise of many waters,</hi> which is heard very far, and makes impressions; the noise of purling streams is grateful, of a roaring sea dreadful, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.15">Rev. i. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.2">xiv. 2</reference>. Christ's gospel, in the glory of which he shines, was to be proclaimed aloud, the report of it to be heard far; to some it is a savour of life, to others of death, according as they are. 2. The brightness of his appearance which he saw: <hi type="italic">The earth shone with his glory;</hi> for God is light, and none can bear the lustre of his light, none <hi type="italic">has seen</hi> nor <hi type="italic">can see it.</hi> Note, That glory of God which shines in the church shines on the world. When God appeared for David <hi type="italic">the brightness that was before him</hi> dispersed the clouds, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.12">Ps. xviii. 12</reference>. This appearance of the glory of God to Ezekiel he observed to be the same with the vision he saw when he first received his commission (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.4">ch. i. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">according to that by the river Chebar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.3">v. 3</reference>); because God is the same, he was pleased to manifest himself in the same manner, for with him is <hi type="italic">no variableness.</hi> "It was the same" (says he) "as that which I saw <hi type="italic">when I came to destroy the city,</hi> that is, to foretel the city's destruction," which he did with such authority and efficacy, and the event did so certainly answer the prediction, that he might be said to destroy it. As a judge, in God's name, he passed a sentence upon it, which was soon executed. God appeared in the same manner when he sent him to speak words of terror and when he sent him to speak words of comfort; for in both God is and will be glorified. <hi type="italic">He kills and he makes alive;</hi> he <hi type="italic">wounds and he heals,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.39">Deut. xxxii. 39</reference>. To the same hand that destroyed we must look for deliverance. <hi type="italic">He has smitten, and he will bind up. Una eademque manus vulnus opemque tulit—The same hand inflicted the wound and healed it.</hi> <div eID="gen19224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19225" type="x-p"/> II. He has a vision of the entrance of this glory into the temple. When he saw this glory he <hi type="italic">fell upon his face</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.3">v. 3</reference>), as not <hi type="italic">able</hi> to bear the lustre of God's glory, or rather as one willing to give him the glory of it by a humble and reverent adoration. But the Spirit <hi type="italic">took him up</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.5">v. 5</reference>) when the <hi type="italic">glory of the Lord</hi> had <hi type="italic">come into the house</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.4">v. 4</reference>), that he might see how the house was filled with it. He saw how the glory of the Lord in this same appearance departed from the temple, because it was profaned, to his great grief; now he shall see it return to the temple to his great satisfaction. See <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.18-Ezek.10.19">ch. x. 18, 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.23">xi. 23</reference>. Note, Though God may forsake his people for a small moment, he will return with everlasting loving-kindness. God's glory <hi type="italic">filled the house</hi> as it had filled the tabernacle which Moses set up and the temple of Solomon, <reference osisRef="Exod.40.34">Exod. xl. 34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.10">1 Kings viii. 10</reference>. Now we do not find that ever the Shechinah did in that manner take possession of the second temple, and therefore this was to have its accomplishment in that glory of the divine grace which shines so brightly in the gospel church, and fills it. Here is no mention of a cloud filling the house as formerly, for we now <hi type="italic">with open face behold the glory of the Lord,</hi> in the face of Christ, and not as of old through the cloud of types. <div eID="gen19225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19226" type="x-p"/> III. He receives instructions more immediately from the glory of the Lord, as Moses did when God had taken possession of the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Lev.1.1">Lev. i. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">I heard him speaking to me out of the house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.6">v. 6</reference>. God's glory shining in the church, we must thence expect to receive divine oracles. <hi type="italic">The man stood by me;</hi> we could not bear to hear the voice of God any more than to see the face of God if Jesus Christ did not stand by us as Mediator. Or, if this was a created angel, it is observable that when God began to speak to Ezekiel he stood by and gave way, having no more to say. Nay, he stood by the prophet, as a learner with him; for <hi type="italic">to the principalities and powers,</hi> to the angels themselves, who <hi type="italic">desire to look into</hi> these things, <hi type="italic">is known by the church the manifold wisdom of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.10">Eph. iii. 10</reference>. The man stood by him to conduct him thither where he might receive further discoveries, <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.1">ch. xliv. 1</reference>.
entries.aaaeb2e96aba94840766b125e68f7090389351c2: <div eID="gen19226" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Temple. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19227" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And he said unto me, Son of man, the place of my throne, and the place of the soles of my feet, where I will dwell in the midst of the children of Israel for ever, and my holy name, shall the house of Israel no more defile, <hi type="italic">neither</hi> they, nor their kings, by their whoredom, nor by the carcases of their kings in their high places. <hi type="super">8</hi> In their setting of their threshold by my thresholds, and their post by my posts, and the wall between me and them, they have even defiled my holy name by their abominations that they have committed: wherefore I have consumed them in mine anger. <hi type="super">9</hi> Now let them put away their whoredom, and the carcases of their kings, far from me, and I will dwell in the midst of them for ever. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thou son of man, shew the house to the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities: and let them measure the pattern. <hi type="super">11</hi> And if they be ashamed of all that they have done, shew them the form of the house, and the fashion thereof, and the goings out thereof, and the comings in thereof, and all the forms thereof, and all the ordinances thereof, and all the forms thereof, and all the laws thereof: and write <hi type="italic">it</hi> in their sight, that they may keep the whole form thereof, and all the ordinances thereof, and do them. <hi type="super">12</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the law of the house; Upon the top of the mountain the whole limit thereof round about <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> most holy. Behold, this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the law of the house. <div eID="gen19227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19228" type="x-p"/> God does here, in effect, renew his covenant with his people Israel, upon his retaking possession of the house, and Ezekiel negotiates the matter, as Moses formerly. This would be of great use to the captives at their return both for direction and encouragement; but it looks further, to those that are blessed with the privileges of the gospel-temple, that they may understand how they are before him on their good behaviour. <div eID="gen19228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19229" type="x-p"/> I. God, by the prophet, puts them in mind of their former provocations, for which they had long lain under the tokens of his displeasure. This conviction is spoken to them to make way for the comforts designed them. Though God <hi type="italic">gives and upbraids not,</hi> it becomes us, when he forgives, to upbraid ourselves with our unworthy conduct towards him. Let them now remember therefore, 1. That they had formerly <hi type="italic">defiled God's holy name,</hi> had profaned and abused all those sacred things by which he had made himself known among them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7">v. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">They and their kings</hi> had brought contempt on the religion they professed, and their relation to God, by their spiritual whoredom, their idolatry, and by worshipping images, which they called <hi type="italic">their kings</hi> (for so <hi type="italic">Moloch</hi> signifies) or lords (for so <hi type="italic">Baal</hi> signifies), but which were really the <hi type="italic">carcases of kings,</hi> not only lifeless and useless, but loathsome and abominable as dead carcases, <hi type="italic">in their high places,</hi> set up in honour of them. They had defiled God's name by their abominations. And what were they? It was <hi type="italic">in setting their threshold by my thresholds, and their post by my posts,</hi> that is, adding their own inventions to God's institutions, and urging all to a compliance with them, as if they had been of equal authority and efficacy, <hi type="italic">teaching for doctrines the commandments of men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.13">Isa. xxix. 13</reference>); or, rather, setting up altars to their idols even in the courts of the temple, than which a more impudent affront could not be put upon the divine Majesty. Thus they set up a separation <hi type="italic">wall between him and them,</hi> which stopped the current of his favours to them and spoiled the acceptableness of their services to him. See what an indignity sinners do to God, setting up their walls in opposition to his, and thrusting him out from what is his right; and see what injury they do to themselves, for the nearer any come to God with their sins the further they set him at a distance from them. Some give this sense of it: Though their houses joined close to God's house, their posts and thresholds to his, so that they were in a manner his next neighbours, <hi type="italic">there was but a wall between me and them</hi> (so it is in the margin), so that it might have been expected they would acquaint themselves with him and be in care to please him, yet they were not so much as neighbourly. Note, It often proves too true, <hi type="italic">The nearer the church the further from God.</hi> They were, by profession, in covenant with God, and yet they had <hi type="italic">defiled the place of his throne</hi> and of <hi type="italic">the soles of his feet,</hi> his temple, where he did both reside and reign. Jerusalem is called the <hi type="italic">city of the great king</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Ps. xlviii. 2</reference>) and his <hi type="italic">footstool,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.99.5">Ps. xcix. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.132.7">cxxxii. 7</reference>. Note, When God's ordinances are profaned his holy name is polluted. 2. That for this God had had a controversy with them in their late troubles. They could not condemn him, for he had but brought upon them the desert of their sins: <hi type="italic">Wherefore I have consumed them in my anger.</hi> Note, Those that pollute God's holy name fall under his just displeasure. <div eID="gen19229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19230" type="x-p"/> II. He calls upon them to repent and reform, and, in order to that, to be ashamed of their iniquities (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Now let them put away their whoredom;</hi> now that they have smarted so severely for it, and now that God is returning in mercy to them and setting up his sanctuary again in the midst of them, now let them cast away their idols and have no more to do with them, that they may not again forfeit the privileges which they have been taught to know the worth of by the want of them. Let them put away their idols, those loathsome <hi type="italic">carcases of their kings, far from me,</hi> from being a provocation to me." This was seasonable counsel now that the prophet had the model or pattern of the temple to set before them; for, 1. If <hi type="italic">they see that pattern,</hi> they will surely be ashamed of their sins (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.10">v. 10</reference>): when they see what mercy God has in store for them, notwithstanding their utter unworthiness of it, they will be ashamed to think of their disingenuous conduct towards him. Note, The goodness of God to us should lead us to repentance, especially to a penitential shame. Let <hi type="italic">them measure the pattern</hi> themselves, and see how much it exceeds the former pattern, and guess by that what great things God has in store for them; and surely it will put them out of countenance to think what the desert of their sins was. And then, 2. If <hi type="italic">they be ashamed</hi> of their sins, they shall surely see more of the pattern, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.11">v. 11</reference>. If they <hi type="italic">be ashamed of all that they have done,</hi> upon a general view of the goodness of God, let them have a more distinct particular account of the temple. Note, Those that improve what they see and know of the goodness of God shall see and know more of it. And then, and not till then, we are qualified for God's favours, when we are truly humbled for our own follies. "<hi type="italic">Show them the form of the house;</hi> let them see what a stately structure it will be; and withal show them the ordinances and laws of it." Note, With the foresights of our comforts it is fit that we should get the knowledge of our duty; with the privileges of God's house we must acquaint ourselves with the rules of it. <hi type="italic">Show them</hi> these ordinances, that they may <hi type="italic">keep them</hi> and <hi type="italic">do them.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> we are made to know our duty, that we may do it, and be blessed in our deed. <div eID="gen19230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19231" type="x-p"/> III. He promises that they shall be such as they should be, and then he will be to them such as they would have him to be, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7">v. 7</reference>. 1. The house of <hi type="italic">Israel shall no more defile my holy name.</hi> This is pure gospel. The precept of the law says, You must not defile my name: the grace of the gospel says, You shall not. Thus what is required in the covenant is promised in the covenant, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.40">Jer. xxxii. 40</reference>. 2. Then <hi type="italic">I will dwell in the midst of them for ever;</hi> and the same again <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.9">v. 9</reference>. God secures to us his good-will by confirming in us his good work. If we do not defile his name, we may be sure that he will not depart from us. <div eID="gen19231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19232" type="x-p"/> IV. The general law of God's house is laid down (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.12">v. 12</reference>), That, whereas formerly only the chancel, or sanctuary, was <hi type="italic">most holy,</hi> now the whole <hi type="italic">mountain of the house</hi> shall be so; the <hi type="italic">whole limit thereof,</hi> including all the courts and all the chambers, shall be as the most holy place, signifying that in gospel-times, 1. The whole church shall have the privilege of the <hi type="italic">holy of holies,</hi> that of a near access to God. All believers have now, under the gospel, <hi type="italic">boldness to enter into the holiest</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.19">Heb. x. 19</reference>), with this advantage, that whereas the high priest entered in the virtue of the blood of bulls and goats, we enter in the virtue of the blood of Jesus, and, wherever we are, we have through him <hi type="italic">access to the Father.</hi> 2. The whole church shall be under a mighty obligation to press towards the perfection of holiness, <hi type="italic">as he who has called us is holy.</hi> All must now be most holy. <hi type="italic">Holiness becomes God's house</hi> for ever, and in gospel-times more than ever. Behold this is the <hi type="italic">law of the house;</hi> let none expect the protection of it that will not submit to this law.
entries.a313e31500ba66723e9ee89cdea716a563a933a3: <div eID="gen19232" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Temple. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19233" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the measures of the altar after the cubits: The cubit <hi type="italic">is</hi> a cubit and a hand breadth; even the bottom <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a cubit, and the breadth a cubit, and the border thereof by the edge thereof round about <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a span: and this <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the higher place of the altar. <hi type="super">14</hi> And from the bottom <hi type="italic">upon</hi> the ground <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the lower settle <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> two cubits, and the breadth one cubit; and from the lesser settle <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the greater settle <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> four cubits, and the breadth <hi type="italic">one</hi> cubit. <hi type="super">15</hi> So the altar <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> four cubits; and from the altar and upward <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> four horns. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the altar <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> twelve <hi type="italic">cubits</hi> long, twelve broad, square in the four squares thereof. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the settle <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> fourteen <hi type="italic">cubits</hi> long and fourteen broad in the four squares thereof; and the border about it <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> half a cubit; and the bottom thereof <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a cubit about; and his stairs shall look toward the east. <hi type="super">18</hi> And he said unto me, Son of man, thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the ordinances of the altar in the day when they shall make it, to offer burnt offerings thereon, and to sprinkle blood thereon. <hi type="super">19</hi> And thou shalt give to the priests the Levites that be of the seed of Zadok, which approach unto me, to minister unto me, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , a young bullock for a sin offering. <hi type="super">20</hi> And thou shalt take of the blood thereof, and put <hi type="italic">it</hi> on the four horns of it, and on the four corners of the settle, and upon the border round about: thus shalt thou cleanse and purge it. <hi type="super">21</hi> Thou shalt take the bullock also of the sin offering, and he shall burn it in the appointed place of the house, without the sanctuary. <hi type="super">22</hi> And on the second day thou shalt offer a kid of the goats without blemish for a sin offering; and they shall cleanse the altar, as they did cleanse <hi type="italic">it</hi> with the bullock. <hi type="super">23</hi> When thou hast made an end of cleansing <hi type="italic">it,</hi> thou shalt offer a young bullock without blemish, and a ram out of the flock without blemish. <hi type="super">24</hi> And thou shalt offer them before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the priests shall cast salt upon them, and they shall offer them up <hi type="italic">for</hi> a burnt offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">25</hi> Seven days shalt thou prepare every day a goat <hi type="italic">for</hi> a sin offering: they shall also prepare a young bullock, and a ram out of the flock, without blemish. <hi type="super">26</hi> Seven days shall they purge the altar and purify it; and they shall consecrate themselves. <hi type="super">27</hi> And when these days are expired, it shall be, <hi type="italic">that</hi> upon the eighth day, and <hi type="italic">so</hi> forward, the priests shall make your burnt offerings upon the altar, and your peace offerings; and I will accept you, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen19233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19234" type="x-p"/> This relates to the altar in this mystical temple, and that is mystical too; for Christ is our altar. The Jews, after their return out of captivity, had an altar long before they had a temple, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.3">Ezra iii. 3</reference>. But this was an altar in the temple. Now here we have, <div eID="gen19234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19235" type="x-p"/> I. The measures of the altar, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.13">v. 13</reference>. It was six yards square at the top and seven yards square at the bottom; it was four yards and a half high; it had a lower bench or shelf, here called a <hi type="italic">settle,</hi> a yard from the ground, on which some of the priests stood to minister, and another two yards above that, on which others of them stood, and these were each of them half a yard broad, and had ledges on either side, that they might stand firmly upon them. The sacrifices were killed at the table spoken of before, <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.39">ch. xl. 39</reference>. What was to be burnt on the altar was given up to those on the lower bench, and handed by them to those on the higher, and they laid it on the altar. Thus in the service of God we must be assistant to one another. <div eID="gen19235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19236" type="x-p"/> II. The ordinances of the altar. Directions are here given, 1. Concerning the dedication of the altar at first. <hi type="italic">Seven days</hi> were to be spent in the dedication of it, and every day sacrifices were to be offered upon it, and particularly a goat for a <hi type="italic">sin-offering</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.25">v. 25</reference>), besides a young bullock for a <hi type="italic">sin-offering</hi> on the first day (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.19">v. 19</reference>), which teaches us in all our religious services to have an eye to Christ the great sin-offering. Neither our persons nor our performances can be acceptable to God unless sin be taken away, and that cannot be taken away but by the blood of Christ, which both sanctifies the altar (for Christ entered by his own blood, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">Heb. ix. 12</reference>) and the gift upon the altar. There were also to be a <hi type="italic">bullock</hi> and a ram offered for a <hi type="italic">burnt-offering</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.24">v. 24</reference>), which was intended purely for the glory of God, to teach us to have an eye to that in all our services; we present ourselves as living sacrifices, and our devotions as spiritual sacrifices, that we and they may be to him for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory. The dedication of the altar is here called the <hi type="italic">cleansing</hi> and <hi type="italic">purging</hi> of it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.20">v. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.26">26</reference>. Christ, our altar, though he had no pollution to be cleansed from, yet sanctified himself (<reference osisRef="John.17.19">John xvii. 19</reference>); and when we consecrate the altars of our hearts to God, to have the fire of holy love always burning upon them, we must see that they be purified and cleansed from the love of the world and the lusts of the flesh. It is observable that there are several differences between the rites of dedication here and those which were appointed <reference osisRef="Exod.29.1-Exod.29.46">Exod. xxix.</reference>, to intimate that the ceremonial institutions were mutable things, and the changes in them were earnests of their period in Christ. Only here, according to the general law, that all the sacrifices must be seasoned with salt (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.13">Lev. ii. 13</reference>), particular orders are given (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.24">v. 24</reference>) that the priests shall <hi type="italic">cast salt upon the sacrifices. Grace</hi> is the <hi type="italic">salt</hi> with which all our religious performances must be seasoned, <reference osisRef="Col.4.6">Col. iv. 6</reference>. An everlasting covenant is called a <hi type="italic">covenant of salt,</hi> because it is incorruptible. The <hi type="italic">glory</hi> reserved for us is incorruptible and undefiled; and the <hi type="italic">grace</hi> wrought in us is the hidden man of the heart in that <hi type="italic">which is not corruptible.</hi> 2. Concerning the constant use that should be made of it, when it was dedicated: <hi type="italic">Henceforward</hi> the priests shall <hi type="italic">make their burnt-offerings and peace-offerings upon this altar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.27">v. 27</reference>), for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> it was <hi type="italic">sanctified,</hi> that it might <hi type="italic">sanctify the gift</hi> that was offered upon it. Observe further, (1.) Who were to serve at the altar: The <hi type="italic">priests of the seed of Zadok,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.19">v. 19</reference>. That family was substituted in the room of Abiathar by Solomon, and God confirms it. His name signifies <hi type="italic">righteous,</hi> for they are the righteous seed that are priests to God, through Christ <hi type="italic">the Lord our righteousness.</hi> (2.) How they should prepare for this service (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall consecrate themselves,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">fill their hand</hi> with the offerings, in token of the giving up of themselves with their offerings to God and to his service. Note, Before we minister to the Lord in holy things we must consecrate ourselves by getting our hands and hearts filled with those things. (3.) How they should speed in it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will accept you.</hi> And if God now accept our works, if our services be pleasing to him, it is enough, we need no more. Those that give themselves to God shall be accepted of God, their persons first and then their performances, through the Mediator.  <chapter eID="Ezek.43"/> <div eID="gen19236" type="x-p"/>

entries.d8921a5330a28ffef55ab47bfc32ee46d36b3695: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11853"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 43</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.43.1-Ezek.43.27">Eze 43:1-27</reference>. Jehovah's Return to the Temple.</title> <div sID="gen21434" type="x-p"/> Everything was now ready for His reception. As the Shekinah glory was the peculiar distinction of the old temple, so it was to be in the new in a degree as much more transcendent as the proportions of the new exceeded those of the old. The fact that the Shekinah glory was not in the second temple proves that it cannot be that temple which is meant in the prophecy.<div eID="gen21434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21435" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11853"/><hi type="bold">2. the way of the east--</hi>the way whereby the glory had departed (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.22">Eze 11:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.23">23</reference>), and rested on Mount Olivet (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.14.4">Zec 14:4</reference>).<div eID="gen21435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21436" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his voice ... like ... many waters--</hi>So English Version rightly, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.24">Eze 1:24</reference>, "voice of the Almighty"; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.15">Re 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.2">14:2</reference>, prove this. Not as Fairbairn translates, "its noise."<div eID="gen21436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21437" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">earth his glory--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.18.1">Re 18:1</reference>). <div eID="gen21437" type="x-p"/>
entries.948a64e10a69f72cecbf376a7f842eb87d27b458: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11854"/><div sID="gen21438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11854"/><hi type="bold">3. when I came to destroy the city--</hi>that is, to pronounce God's word for its destruction. So completely did the prophets identify themselves with Him in whose name they spake. <div eID="gen21438" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c460c1c5af071214e9a180dacfdb6c447527c6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11855"/><div sID="gen21439" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11855"/><hi type="bold">6. the man--</hi>who had been measuring the buildings (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.3">Eze 40:3</reference>). <div eID="gen21439" type="x-p"/>
entries.69058843ea285736b62d559bb2e38a1be0e8e7b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11856"/><div sID="gen21440" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11856"/><hi type="bold">7. the place--</hi>that is, "behold the place of My throne"--the place on which your thoughts have so much dwelt (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.1-Isa.2.3">Is 2:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.16-Zech.14.20">Zec 14:16-20</reference>; Mal 3:1). God from the first claimed to be their King politically as well as religiously: and He had resisted their wish to have a human king, as implying a rejection of Him as the proper Head of the state. Even when He yielded to their wish, it was with a protest against their king ruling except as His vicegerent. When Messiah shall reign at Jerusalem, He shall then first realize the original idea of the theocracy, with its at once divine and human king reigning in righteousness over a people all righteous (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.12">Eze 43:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.1">Is 52:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.54.13">54:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.21">60:21</reference>). <div eID="gen21440" type="x-p"/>
entries.12c5e7aa74fbd8f2ca5ea4fe855c23c67d0d16a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11857"/><div sID="gen21441" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11857"/><hi type="bold">9. carcasses of their kings--</hi>It is supposed that some of their idolatrous kings were buried within the bounds of Solomon's temple [Henderson]. Rather, "the carcasses of their idols," here called "kings," as having had lordship over them in past times (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.13">Is 26:13</reference>); but henceforth Jehovah, alone their rightful lord, shall be their king, and the idols that had been their "king" would appear but as "carcasses." Hence these defunct kings are associated with the "high places" in <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7">Eze 43:7</reference> [Fairbairn]. <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Le 26:30</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.16.18">Jr 16:18</reference>, confirm this. Manasseh had built altars in the courts of the temple to the host of heaven (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.5">2Ki 21:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.6">23:6</reference>).<div eID="gen21441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21442" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will dwell in the midst ... for ever--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Re 21:3</reference>). <div eID="gen21442" type="x-p"/>
entries.24ab98e0ec75a8460162ad1a87fe9d6a27161089: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11858"/><div sID="gen21443" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11858"/><hi type="bold">10. show the house ... that they may be ashamed of their iniquities--</hi>When the spirituality of the Christian scheme is shown to men by the Holy Ghost, it makes them "ashamed of their iniquities." <div eID="gen21443" type="x-p"/>
entries.661af330f53396b2c459675320ac3832128eb4e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11859"/><div sID="gen21444" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11859"/><hi type="bold">12. whole ... most holy--</hi>This superlative, which had been used exclusively of the holy of holies (<reference osisRef="Exod.26.34">Ex 26:34</reference>), was now to characterize the entire building. This all-pervading sanctity was to be "the law of the (whole) house," as distinguished from the Levitical law, which confined the peculiar sanctity to a single apartment of it. <div eID="gen21444" type="x-p"/>
entries.715b020f30ed1560863c2514474e79322c3e06fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11860"/><div sID="gen21445" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11860"/>13-27. As to the altar of burnt offering, which was the appointed means of access to God. <div eID="gen21445" type="x-p"/>

entries.0de752ffa1567fd320e31beda9057ed36f617bc4: <div eID="gen32532" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32533" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32534" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32534" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32533" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32535" type="x-p"/> The glory of the Lord is represented as returning to the temple, <reference osisRef="Eze.43.1-Eze.43.6">Eze 43:1-6</reference>; where God promises to fix his residence, if the people repent and forsake those sins which caused him to depart from them, <reference osisRef="Eze.43.7-Eze.43.12">Eze 43:7-12</reference>. Then the measures of the altar, and the ordinances relating to it, are set down, <reference osisRef="Eze.43.13-Eze.43.27">Eze 43:13-27</reference>.
entries.00caf7994adf629144a6bef36e862136ebb0334a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32536" type="x-p"/> The glory of the God of Israel came from the way of the east - This was the chariot of cherubim, wheels, etc., which he saw at the river Chebar. And this glory, coming from the east, is going to enter into the eastern gate of the temple, and thence to shine out upon the whole earth. Is there not a mystery here? All knowledge, all religion, and all arts and sciences, have traveled, according to the course of the sun, From East To West! From that quarter the Divine glory at first came; and thence the rays of Divine light continue to diffuse themselves over the face of the earth. From thence came the Bible, and through that the new covenant. From thence came the prophets, the apostles, and the first missionaries, that brought the knowledge of God to Europe, to the isles of the sea, and to the west first, and afterwards to these northern regions.
entries.8fa58ef15995b1fd142ea8fb2479b4c60920bcac: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen32536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32537" type="x-p"/> The spirit took me up - And, to follow this thought for a moment, how many men has this heavenly Spirit taken up; filled them with his own influence, and sent them to every country, and nation, and tongue, and people, to testify the Gospel of the grace of God, and to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ! What spiritual temples have been raised, beautified, and filled with the glory of God! And this light is shining and burning more and more unto the perfect day, when the whole earth shall be filled with the glory of God!
entries.a6f45f5d7b81be193e57389a76a9732990248a81: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen32537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32538" type="x-p"/> Son of man, the place of my throne - The throne refers to his majesty; the soles of his feet, to his condescension in dwelling among men. <div eID="gen32538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32539" type="x-p"/> Where I will dwell in the midst of the children of Israel - The tabernacle and temple were types of the incarnation of Jesus Christ: "Destroy This Temple, and after three days I will raise it up; - but this he spake of the temple of his body;" <reference osisRef="Joh.2.19">Joh 2:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.2.21">Joh 2:21</reference>. And in That Temple "dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily." Into this immaculate humanity did the glory of the Supreme God enter; and thus, "God was in Christ reconciling the world unto himself." And this Jesus is Immanuel, God with Us. In him we find united the ineffable majesty of God, with the abjectness of man. He humbled himself in human nature, not only to bear the form of a servant, but to suffer death upon the cross as a malefactor slave! But by these means he has purchased eternal redemption for us; and the spiritual Israel, who find redemption in his blood, shall be raised up wherever his holy name shall be proclaimed; and shall not, like the old apostate Israel, defile that great name by idolatry or a life of wickedness, but they shall show forth the virtues of Him who has called them from darkness into his marvellous light.
entries.e742dd6d7d5c921689663659eaf5ffd93997872c: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen32539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32540" type="x-p"/> In their setting of their threshold - They had even gone so far as to set up their idol altars by those of Jehovah; so that their abominable idols were found in the very house of God! therefore, "he consumed them in his anger."
entries.c375e939d73faba1cdf5ae4d001603c8affde848: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen32540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32541" type="x-p"/> Now let them put away their whoredom - Their idolatry. <div eID="gen32541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32542" type="x-p"/> And the carcasses of their kings - It appears that God was displeased with their bringing their kings so near his temple. David was buried in the city of David, which was on Mount Zion, near to the temple; and so were almost all the kings of Judah; but God requires that the place of his temple and its vicinity shall be kept unpolluted; and when they put away all kinds of defilement, then will he dwell among them.
entries.ace121f63f842af428b9394d16ef5a20843ffdfa: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen32542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32543" type="x-p"/> Show the house to the house of Israel - Show them this holy house where the holy God dwells, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities. Their name, their profession, their temple, their religious services, all bound them to a holy life; all within them, all without them, should have been holiness unto the Lord. But alas! they have been bound by no ties, and they have sinned against all their obligations; nevertheless, let them measure the pattern, let them see the rule by which they should have walked, and let them measure themselves by this standard, and walk accordingly.
entries.36dabaa1a8da63739b916f8b88481513f6ef8c05: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen32543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32544" type="x-p"/> And if they be ashamed - If, in a spirit of true repentance, they acknowledge their past transgressions, and purpose in his help never more to offend their God, then teach them every thing that concerns my worship, and their profiting by it.
entries.8bbd3a7e3e5d753f62b3cbb473de3b1e497a6fa0: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen32544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32545" type="x-p"/> This is the law of the house - From the top of the mountain on which it stands, to the bottom, all round about, all shall be holy; no buildings shall be erected in any part, nor place nor spot be appropriated to a common use; all shall be considered as being most holy.
entries.2cecec51ac52d31e9dd39a1f940d78863bc480b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen32545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32546" type="x-p"/> The cubit is a cubit and a hand breadth - It is the same cubit by which all the previous admeasurements were made, and was a hand breadth or four inches longer than the Babylonian cubit.
entries.50261cf5e486c9c9dae120e9c778f03beb9c1890: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen32546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32547" type="x-p"/> So the altar - ההראל haharel, "the mount of God." <div eID="gen32547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32548" type="x-p"/> And from the altar - ומהאראיל umihaariel, "and from the lion of God." Perhaps the first was a name given to the altar when elevated to the honor of God, and on which the victims were offered to him, and the second, the lion of God, may mean the hearth, which might have been thus called, because it devoured and consumed the burnt-offerings, as a lion does his prey. See on <reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">Isa 29:1</reference> (note).
entries.a6c6ac32baf7fd13ac31b0f977c05baf94d2ac06: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32549" type="x-p"/> And the settle - The ledge on which the priests walked round the altar, see <reference osisRef="Eze.43.14">Eze 43:14</reference>. By these settles or ledges the altar was narrowed towards the top. "The ascent shall look toward the east;" this ascent was an inclined plane. But these settles, or more properly ledges, as Bp. Newcome translates, may be thus computed. The altar itself was ten feet high and twenty broad; the same as that of Solomon, <reference osisRef="2Chr.4.1">2Chr 4:1</reference>. <div eID="gen32549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32550" type="x-p"/> Height Cubits For the base, <reference osisRef="Eze.43.13">Eze 43:13</reference>, is in height 1 From the surface of the base to the first ledge, <reference osisRef="Eze.43.14">Eze 43:14</reference> 1 From the lower ledge to the upper, <reference osisRef="Eze.43.14">Eze 43:14</reference> 4 From the upper ledge to the ariel or hearth, <reference osisRef="Eze.43.15">Eze 43:15</reference> 4 In all 10 Breadth Cubits And as to the breadth, the upper ledge, <reference osisRef="Eze.43.17">Eze 43:17</reference>, was 14 Add a cubit on each side for the higher ledge, <reference osisRef="Eze.43.14">Eze 43:14</reference>, latter part 2 Add a cubit on each side for the lower ledge, <reference osisRef="Eze.43.14">Eze 43:14</reference>, former part 2 Add a cubit on each side for the base, <reference osisRef="Eze.43.13">Eze 43:13</reference> 2 In all 20 <div eID="gen32550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32551" type="x-p"/> The altar of burnt-offerings, described <reference osisRef="Exo.27.1">Exo 27:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.38.1">Exo 38:1</reference>, was smaller than this, because it was to be removed from place to place with the tabernacle. This was designed for a permanent temple. See Bp. Newcome on this chapter.
entries.f84007080a7ec7d1cbb049c807a83d9fb6859549: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen32551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32552" type="x-p"/> The priests - that be of the seed of Zadok - It was this Zadok that was put in the place of Abiathar, by Solomon, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.35">1Kgs 2:35</reference>, in whose family the priesthood had continued ever since.
entries.d7ca4326d3fd50622dfab11fc6139b5c68528089: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen32552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32553" type="x-p"/> Seven days shalt thou prepare - These are, in general, ordinances of the Law; and may be seen by consulting the parallel passages. All these directions are given that they might follow them, when they should be put in possession of their own land. For in several cases the prophet enters into particulars, as if he had supposed that the book of the law had perished.  <chapter eID="Ezek.43"/> <div eID="gen32553" type="x-p"/>

entries.f1b0af259fcf5ac686997143b45eb572508ae553: <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.1-Ezek.43.12">Eze 43:1-12</reference> <div eID="gen15303" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Entrance of the Glory of the Lord into the New Temple</title> <div sID="gen15304" type="x-p"/> Eze 43:1. <hi type="italic">And he led me to the gate, the gate which looked toward the east:</hi> Eze 43:2. <hi type="italic">And behold the glory of the God of Israel came from the east, and its sound was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with His glory.</hi> Eze 43:3. <hi type="italic">And the appearance which I saw, was to look at like the appearance which I saw when I came to destroy the city; and (there were) appearances like the appearance which I had seen by the river Chebar; and I fell down upon my face.</hi> Eze 43:4. <hi type="italic">And the glory of Jehovah came into the house by the way of the gate, the direction of which is toward the east.</hi> Eze 43:5. <hi type="italic">And wind lifted me up and brought me into the inner court; and, behold, the glory of Jehovah filled the house.</hi> Eze 43:6. <hi type="italic">And I heard one speaking to me from the house, and there was a man standing by me.</hi> Eze 43:7. <hi type="italic">And he said to me, Son of man, the place of my throne and the place of the soles of my feet, where I shall dwell in the midst of the sons of Israel for ever; and the house of Israel will no more defile my holy name, they and their kings, through their whoredom and through the corpses of their kings, their high places,</hi> Eze 43:8. <hi type="italic">When they set their threshold by my threshold, and their door-posts by my door-posts, and there was only the wall between me and them, and they defiled my holy name by their abominations which they did, so that I destroyed them in my wrath.</hi> Eze 43:9. <hi type="italic">Now will they remove their whoredom and the corpses of their kings from me, and I shall dwell in the midst of them for ever.</hi> Eze 43:10. <hi type="italic">Thou, son of man, show to the house of Israel this house, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities, and may measure the well-measured building.</hi> Eze 43:11. <hi type="italic">And when they are ashamed of all that they have done, show them the picture of the house and its arrangement, and its goings out and in, and all its forms and all its statutes, and all its forms and all its laws; and write it before their eyes, that they may keep all its form and all its statutes and do them.</hi> Eze 43:12. <hi type="italic">This is the law of the house: Upon the top of the mountain all its territory round about is most holy. Behold, this is the law of the house.</hi> - The angel had shown the prophet the new sanctuary as already completed, and had measured it in his presence according to its several parts. But this building only became the house of God when Jehovah as the God of Israel consecrated it, to be the dwelling-place of His divine and gracious presence in the midst of His people, by the entrance of His divine glory into the house.<note placement="foot">“The Lord appears, and fills the house with His own glory; showing that the house will not only be built, but will be filled with the power of God” (Theodoret).</note> <div eID="gen15304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15305" type="x-p"/> The description of the new temple closes, therefore, with this act of consecration. That the prophet might see this act of divine grace with his own eyes, the measuring man led him from the ground surrounding the temple (<reference osisRef="Ezek.42.15-Ezek.42.20">Eze 42:15-20</reference>) back again to the east gate (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.1">Eze 43:1</reference>). The allusion is to the eastern gate of the outer court; for it is not till <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.5">Eze 43:5</reference> that Ezekiel is taken into the inner court, and, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.1">Eze 44:1</reference>, he was brought <hi type="italic">back</hi> to the east gate of the outer court. Standing in front of this gate, he sees the glory of the God of Israel come by the way from the east with a great noise, and lighting up the earth with its splendour. The coming of the theophany from the east points back to <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.19">Eze 10:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.1">Eze 11:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.23">Eze 11:23</reference>, where the Shechinah, when leaving the ancient temple, went out at the east gate and ascended to the summit of the mountain, which was situated on the east of Jerusalem. It was from the east, therefore, that it returned to enter the new temple. This fact is sufficient of itself to show that the present entrance of the divine glory into the new temple did not lay the foundation for a new and more exalted bond of grace, but was simply intended to restore the relation which had existed before the removal of Israel into captivity. The tabernacle and Solomon’s temple had both been consecrated by Jehovah in the same manner as the seat of His throne of grace in Israel (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.40.34-Exod.40.35">Exo 40:34-35</reference>; 1Ki 8:10-11; and <reference osisRef="2Chr.5.13-2Chr.5.14">2Ch 5:13-14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.1-2Chr.7.3">2Ch 7:1-3</reference>, from which the expression את־בּית in <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.5">Eze 43:5</reference> has been borrowed). It is true that Hävernick, Kliefoth, and others find, along with this agreement, a difference in the fact that the glory of Jehovah appeared in the cloud in both the tabernacle and Solomon’s temple; whereas here, on the contrary, it appeared in that peculiar form which Ezekiel had already repeatedly seen. But it does not follow that there was really a difference, because the cloud is not mentioned in the verses before us; for it is evident that the cloud was not wanting, even in the manifestation of the glory of God seen by Ezekiel, from the words found in <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.3">Eze 10:3</reference> : “The <hi type="italic">cloud</hi> filled the inner court, and the glory of Jehovah had risen up from the cherubim to the threshold of the house, <hi type="italic">and the house was filled with the cloud</hi>, and the court was full of the splendour of the glory of Jehovah.” If, therefore, it is expressly attested in <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.3">Eze 43:3</reference>, as even Kliefoth admits, that the appearance of God which entered the temple as like the appearance which Ezekiel saw by the Chaboras and before the destruction of the temple, and in connection with the last-mentioned appearance the cloud was visible along with the brilliant splendour of the divine <hi type="italic">doxa</hi>, the cloud will certainly not have been wanting when it entered the new temple; and the only reason why it is not expressly mentioned must be, that it did not present a contrast to the brilliant splendour, or tend to obscure the light of the glory of God, but as a shining cloud was simply the atmospheric clothing of the theophany. <div eID="gen15305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15306" type="x-p"/> If, then, the cloud did not present a contrast to the brilliancy of the divine glory, it cannot be inferred from the words, “and the earth shone with His glory,” that there was any difference between this and the earlier manifestations of the divine glory at the consecration of the tabernacle and Solomon’s temple; more especially as these words to not affirm that it became light on earth, but simply that the earth shone with the glory God, - that is to say, that it threw a bright light upon the earth as it passed along, - so that this remark simply serves to indicate the intensity of the brightness of this theophany. The words 'קולו כקול  are not to be understood, as we may learn from <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.24">Eze 1:24</reference>, as referring to a voice of the coming God, but describe the loud noise made by the moving of the theophany on account of the rustling of the wings of the cherubim. This resembled the roaring of mighty waves. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.3">Eze 43:3</reference>, the expression וּכּמראה המּראה ...כּמּראה  is somewhat heavy in style, but is correct Hebrew; and the remark with which Hitzig seeks to justify his alteration of וכמראה into ומראה, - namely, that כמראה “would signify 'so the appearance,' whereas Ezekiel intends to explain the present appearance from the well-known earlier one,” - is false so far as the usage of the language is concerned. When the Hebrew uses two כּ in cases of comparison, which we are accustomed to express in German by <hi type="italic">so...wie</hi> (so...as), he always commences with the thing to which he compares another, and lets the thing which is to be compared follow afterwards. Thus, for example, in <reference osisRef="Gen.18.25">Gen 18:25</reference>, והיה  does not affirm that it happens as to the righteous so to the wicked, but <hi type="italic">vice versâ</hi>, that it happens to the righteous as to the wicked; and in <reference osisRef="Gen.44.18">Gen 44:18</reference>, כּי כמוך  does not mean, for like thee so is Pharaoh, but “for thou art like Pharaoh.” According to this genuine Hebrew expression, the present appearance of the divine glory is mentioned first in the verse before us, and then in the earlier one which the present resembled. And even the apparent pleonasm מראה המּראה vanishes if we render מראה by “look,” - the look of the apparition which I saw was just like the apparition, etc. 'כּבאי לשׁחת וגו refers to the ecstatic transportation of the prophet to Jerusalem (Ezekiel 8-11), to witness the destruction of the city (see more particularly <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.4">Eze 8:4</reference>; Eze 9:1.). “The prophet destroyed the city ideally by his prophecy, of which the fulfilment simply forms the objective reverse side” (Hitzig). וּמראות is appended in loose apposition, - there were appearances, visions, - and the plural is to be taken as in מראות אלהים in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.1">Eze 1:1</reference>; Eze 40:2. For what follows, compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.23">Eze 3:23</reference>; Eze 10:15. For <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.43.5">Eze 43:5</reference></hi>, compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.14">Eze 3:14</reference>; Eze 11:24. <div eID="gen15306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15307" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.6">Eze 43:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7">Eze 43:7</reference> the question arises, who it is who is speaking to the prophet; whether it is Jehovah, who has entered the temple, or the man who is standing by Ezekiel in the inner court? There can be no doubt that מדּבּר is Jehovah here, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.2.2">Eze 2:2</reference>; though the commentators are divided in opinion whether Jehovah spoke directly to the prophet, or through the medium of the man who stood by his side. Hävernick presses the <hi type="italic">Hithpael</hi> מדּבּר, and imagines that Ezekiel heard God conversing within the sanctuary, in consequence of which the angel stood by his side; so that the words of God consisted chiefly in the command to communicate to Ezekiel the divine revelation which follows in Eze 43:7. But this view is proved to be erroneous by the expression אלי which follows מדּבּר, and which Hävernick has overlooked. Kliefoth, on the other hand, is of opinion that the words contained in <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7">Eze 43:7</reference>, which proceeded from the מדּבּר, were addressed to the prophet directly by God Himself; for he heard them before anything was said by the man, and neither here nor in what follows is the man said to have spoken. On the contrary, both here and in what follows, even in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.20">Eze 46:20</reference>,<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.24">Eze 46:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.6-Ezek.47.7">Eze 47:6-7</reference>, it is always God Himself who appears as the speaker, and the man simply as the prophet’s guide. But this is also not correct. Such passages as <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.20">Eze 46:20</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.24">Eze 46:24</reference> compared with <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.19">Eze 43:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.21">Eze 43:21</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.6">Eze 47:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.8">Eze 47:8</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.1">Eze 43:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.4">Eze 43:4</reference>, show undeniably that the man who conducted the prophet also talked with him. Consequently, in the case referred to in the verse before us, we must also conclude that he who spoke to the prophet from the temple addressed him through the medium of the man who stood by his side, and that אישׁ is the subject to ויּאמר in <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7">Eze 43:7</reference>; from which, however, it by no means follows that the מדּבּר was also an angel, who spoke to the prophet, not from the most holy place, but simply from within the house, as Hitzig explains the matter. The meaning is rather, that Ezekiel heard God conversing with him from the sanctuary, whilst a man, i.e., an angel, stood by his side and spoke to him as follows. אישׁ is in that case not some angel merely who spoke in the name of Jehovah, but the angel of Jehovah, God’s own speaker, ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ (Joh 1:1.). But according to his outward <hi type="italic">habitus</hi>, this angel of the Lord, who is designated as אישׁ, is identical with the angel who showed the prophet the temple, and measured it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.40.3">Eze 40:3</reference> onwards). For according to Eze 47:1. this אישׁ had also a measuring rod, and measured. The absence of the article from אישׁ in <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.6">Eze 43:6</reference>, which prevents Kliefoth from admitting this identity, does not indicate decidedly that a different man from the one mentioned before is introduced here as the prophet’s attendant, but simply leaves the identity of this אישׁ with the former indefinite, so that it can only be inferred from the further course of events; because the point of importance here was neither to establish this identity by employing the article, nor to define the medium of the word of God more precisely, but simply to introduce the words which follow as the words of God Himself. The address commences with an explanation on the part of God that the temple into which the glory of the Lord had entered was the place of His throne, where He would dwell for ever among the sons of Israel. The את־מקום is a concise expression, in which את is <hi type="italic">nota accus</hi>., and we have to supply in thought either ראה or הנּה: “behold the place.” מקום כּפּות רגלי, the place of the soles of my feet (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.60.13">Isa 60:13</reference>), is equivalent to the footstool of my feet in Isa 66:1. The ark of the covenant is called the footstool of God in <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.2">1Ch 28:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.132.7">Psa 132:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.99.5">Psa 99:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lam.2.1">Lam 2:1</reference>, where this epithet may possibly be used to designate the temple. This also applies to the throne of Jehovah, since God was enthroned above the cherubim of the ark in the holy of holies (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.25.22">Exo 25:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.4">1Sa 4:4</reference>, etc.). In the sanctuary which Ezekiel saw, no reference is made to the ark of the covenant, and the silence with regard to this is hardly to be regarded as a mere omission to mention it, inasmuch as none of the things contained in the temple are mentioned with the exception of the altars, not even the table of shew-bread or the candlestick. The ark of the covenant is not mentioned, because, as is stated in <reference osisRef="Jer.3.16">Jer 3:16</reference>, in the Messianic times the ark of the covenant will not be remembered, neither will it be missed. לעולם, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.26">Eze 37:26</reference> and Eze 37:28. The promise culminates in this. לעולם does not apply either to the tabernacle or to Solomon’s temple, in which Jehovah also had His dwelling-place, though not for ever. These sanctuaries He left, and gave them up to destruction, because the Israelites had profaned His holy name by their idolatry. This will not take place any more after the erection of the new sanctuary. לא יטמּאוּ is not imperative, but a simple future: “they will no more defiled,” because they come to a knowledge of their sins through the punitive judgment of exile, so that they become ashamed of them, and because the Lord will have poured out His Spirit upon them (cf. Eze 37:23., <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.29">Eze 39:29</reference>). - Formerly, however (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7">Eze 43:7</reference></hi>), they profaned the holy name of God by their spiritual whoredom (cf. Ezekiel 16) and by dead idols, for which they erected high places in the immediate neighbourhood of the dwelling-place of Jehovah, that is to say, even in the temple courts, so that Jehovah was only separated from the idols by a wall. This is the general meaning of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7">Eze 43:7</reference></hi> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.8">Eze 43:8</reference>, in which the exposition of פּגרי  is difficulty. Rosenmüller, Hävernick, and others understand by the “corpses of their kings,” the dead idols. Ewald, Hitzig, and Kliefoth, on the other hand, take the expression in a literal sense, as referring to the corpses of kings which had been buried near to the temple, so that the temple had been defiled by the proximity of these graves. But the latter view is precluded by the fact that not a single instance can be adduced of the burial of a king in the vicinity of the temple, since <reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Neh 3:15</reference> contains no allusion to anything of the kind, and the tombs of the kings upon Zion were not so near to the temple that it could possibly be defiled in consequence. Moreover, בּמותם cannot be reconciled with this view; and for that reason Ewald and Hitzig propose to read בּמותם, “in their death.” The attempt of Kliefoth, however, to defend the reading בּמותם, by taking it as in apposition to בּזנוּתם and not to וּבפּגרי מלכיהם, is a desperate remedy, which clearly shows the impossibility of connecting בּמותם with the “corpses of the kings.” We therefore understand by פּגרי the dead idols, in accordance with <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.16.18">Jer 16:18</reference>); but by מלכיהם we understand, not the idols, but the Israelitish kings, as in the case of the preceding מלכיהם; partly because it cannot be shown that the plural מלכים is ever used in the sense of idols (though the singular מלכּם is used of Baal in Zep 1:5 and <reference osisRef="Amos.5.26">Amo 5:26</reference>), and partly on account of the harshness involved in interpreting the two מלכיהם when standing so close together, in the first instance of the kings, and in the second of the idols of Israel. The corpses of the kings are therefore the dead idols, for which the kings (for example, Manasseh) had built altars or high places (בּמות) in the sanctuary, i.e., in the courts of the temple (2Ki 21:4-7). The objection that פּגרים without anything further, such, for instance, as גּלּוּלים sa ,ecnatsni rof ,hcus in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference>, cannot signify the dead idols, will not bear examination, as the more precise definition which is wanting is supplied by the context, where idolatry is the point in question. בּמותם without the preposition ב is a loosely attached apposition to בּפּגרי מלכיהם and בּזנוּתם, which defines more precisely in what way the whoredom of the nation and the dead idols of the kings had amounted to a defiling of the house of the Lord, namely, from the fact that the people and the kings had erected temples of high places (<hi type="italic">bâmoth</hi>) for dead idols by the side of the temple of the living God, and had placed them so close that the threshold and door-posts of these idol-temples touched the threshold and door-posts of the temple of Jehovah, and there was nothing but the wall of the temple (הקיר) between Jehovah and the carcase-gods. בּמותם is explained in this way in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.43.8">Eze 43:8</reference></hi>, and then the defiling of the holy name of the Lord is mentioned again for the purpose of appending, by means of ואכל (imperf. <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> of כלה), the allusion to the penal judgment which they had thereby brought upon themselves. Eze 43:9. Such profanation as this will not take place any more in time to come, and Jehovah will dwell for ever in the midst of Israel. <div eID="gen15307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15308" type="x-p"/> To lead Israel to this goal, Ezekiel is to show them the house (i.e., the temple). In this way are the further words of God in <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.10-Ezek.43.12">Eze 43:10-12</reference> attached to what goes before. הגּיד את־הבּית, show or make known the house, is equivalent to proclaim to the people the revelation concerning the new temple. In this were the Israelites to discern the magnitude of the grace of God, that they might blush at their evil deeds, and measure the well-measured building (תּכנית, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.12">Eze 28:12</reference>), i.e., carefully consider and ponder what the Lord had bestowed upon His people through this sanctuary, so that they might suffer themselves to be brought to repentance by means of its glory. And if they felt shame and repentance on account of their transgressions, Ezekiel was to show them the shape and arrangement of the sanctuary, with all its forms and ordinances, an write them out before their eyes, that they might have the picture of it impressed upon their minds, and keep the statutes thereof. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.11">Eze 43:11</reference> the words are crowded together, to indicate that all the several parts and arrangements of the new temple are significant and worthy of being pondered and laid to heart. צוּרה is the shape of the temple generally, its external form; תּכוּנה, the internal arrangement as a whole. Both of these are noticed specifically by the allusion to the goings out and in, as well as to the forms (צוּרות) of the separate parts, and their statutes and laws. חקּות are the precepts concerning the things to be observed by Israel when appearing before the Lord in the temple, the regulations for divine worship. תּורות, the instructions contained in these statutes for sanctification of life. The second וכל־צוּרתו is omitted in the lxx and some of the Hebrew <hi type="italic">Codd</hi>., and has therefore been expunged as a gloss by Dathe, Hitzig, and other critics; but it is undoubtedly genuine, and in conformity with the intentional crowding together of words. - The admonition to keep and to observe everything carefully is closed in <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.12">Eze 43:12</reference> with a statement of the fundamental law of the temple; that upon the lofty mountain the whole of its domain round about is to be most holy. על־ראשׁ ההר does not belong to הבּית ot g in the sense of the house which is to be built upon the top of the mountain, but to the contents of the <hi type="italic">thorâh</hi> of this house. It is to stand upon the top of the mountain, and to be most holy in all its domain. ראשׁ ההר is to be understood in accordance with <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.2">Eze 40:2</reference>; and גּבלו points back to הבּית. Both by its situation upon a very high mountain, and also by the fact that not merely the inner sanctuary, and not merely the whole of the temple house, but also the whole of its surroundings (all its courts), are to be most holy, the new sanctuary is to be distinguished from the earlier one. What has been already stated - namely, that the temple shall not be profaned any more - is compressed into this clause; and by the repetition of the words, “this is the law of the house,”' the first section of this vision, viz., the description of the temple, is rounded off; whilst the command given to the prophet in <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.10">Eze 43:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.11">Eze 43:11</reference>, to make known all the statutes and laws of this temple to the house of Israel, forms at the same time the transition to the section which follows.
entries.334a27a53063be992fd94a8156d325bfe63ec7ca: <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.13-Ezek.43.17">Eze 43:13-17</reference> <div eID="gen15308" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Description and Consecration of the Altar of Burnt-Offering</title> <title type="x-s2">Description of the Altar</title> <div sID="gen15309" type="x-p"/> Eze 43:13. <hi type="italic">And these are the measures of the altar in cubits: The cubit a cubit and a handbreadth; a ground-framework of a cubit (in height), and a cubit in breadth, and its moulding on its border round about a span. This is the base of the altar.</hi> Eze 43:14. <hi type="italic">And from the ground-framework of earth to the lower enclosure, two cubits (in height), and a cubit in breadth; and from the small enclosure to the greater enclosure, four cubits (in height), and one cubit in breadth.</hi> Eze 43:15. <hi type="italic">And the mount of God, four cubits; and from the heart of God upwards, the four horns.</hi> Eze 43:16. <hi type="italic">And the hearth of God, twelve cubits in length by twelve cubits in breadth; squared on its four sides.</hi> Eze 43:17. <hi type="italic">And the enclosure, fourteen cubits in length by fourteen cubits in breadth on its four sides; and the moulding round about it, half a cubit; and the ground-framework of it, a cubit round about: and its steps faced the east.</hi> - To the heading, “these are the measures of the altar in (according to) cubits,” there is once more appended, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.5">Eze 40:5</reference>, in connection with the measuring of the temple, the length of the cubit measure. The description commences with the foundation of the altar, and, proceeding upwards, gives the height and breadth of the several gradations of the walls of the altar, up to the horns at the four corners (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.13-Ezek.43.15">Eze 43:13-15</reference>). It then passes from above downwards, to supply the length and breadth or the circumference of the different stages (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.16">Eze 43:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.17">Eze 43:17</reference>). As the first, or lowest part, the חיק is mentioned, literally, the bosom or lap; then by transference, the hollow formed by the sides of a chariot (1Ki 22:35); here the lower hollow or base of the altar (<hi type="italic">p</hi>), formed by a border of a definite height, to merely “a frame running round, a stand in which the altar stood” (Hitzig), nor merely “the hollow filled with earth” (Kliefoth), but both together. This ground-framework (<hi type="italic">p</hi>) was a cubit (sc., high) and a cubit broad. That האמּה is to be taken as referring to the height, is evident from the statement of the breadth which follows. חיק האמּה is not to be altered into חיקהּ אמּה, as Ewald proposes, nor is האמּה to be changed into באמּה (Hitzig); but Hävernick’s explanation is to be adopted: “and a bosom (was there) the cubit,” i.e., of the height of the cubit just described. רחב, breadth, is the extent to which the bosom projected beyond the next enclosure (<hi type="italic">q</hi>) on every side, and formed a support, the circumference of which was a cubit more than the lower cube of the altar on every side. This is shown by the measurements in <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.16">Eze 43:16</reference> and Eze 43:17. The חיק had a גּבוּל on its שׂפה of a span (half a cubit) in height (<hi type="italic">o</hi>). שׂפה, lip, is the rim (1Ki 7:26; <reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">Gen 22:17</reference>); and גּבוּל, the bordering on the rim, is a moulding. The feminine suffixes attached to גּבוּלהּ and שׂפתהּ refer to חיק, which is of the masculine gender, no doubt, when used in its literal sense of bosom or lap, but is construed as a feminine in the tropical sense of an inanimate object. The ground-framework, with its moulding, formed the גּב of the altar. גּב, the arched, then a hump or back, signifies here the support of the altar. Upon this support the altar rose in a cubical enclosure or frame, which diminished in circumference by ledges or steps. The enclosure resting upon the support, and therefore the lowest enclosure (<hi type="italic">q</hi>), is mentioned in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.43.14">Eze 43:14</reference></hi>; and the one which followed (<hi type="italic">r</hi>) in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.43.14">Eze 43:14</reference></hi>. <div eID="gen15309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15310" type="x-p"/> The word עזרה, which has probably sprung from עצר by the softening of צ into ז, signifies enclosure, surrounding, and is mostly used for the outer court of the temple; here it is applied to the altar, and signifies the enclosure or framework of the kernel of the altar, consisting of earth. As the altar rose in steps, a distinction is made between the lower or smaller, and the (upper or) greater עזרה. The identity of the lower עזרה and the smaller one (הקּטנּה) is so evident from the course of the description, that it is universally admitted by modern expositors. The lower one (<hi type="italic">q</hi>) is called the small one, in comparison with the large one which stood above it, from the fact that its height was smaller, as it was only two cubits high, whereas the upper one (<hi type="italic">r</hi>) was four. When, therefore, the measurement of the greater one is given in this way in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.43.14">Eze 43:14</reference></hi>: “from the small enclosure to the great enclosure, four cubits,” this statement cannot be understood in any other way than as meaning, that this enclosure or frame had a height of four cubits from the lower to the upper end, - that is to say, in other words, that the lower ledge was four cubits from the upper. Consequently the statement in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.43.14">Eze 43:14</reference></hi>, “from the ground-framework of earth to the lower enclosure, two cubits,” can also have no other meaning than that the lower enclosure, from the lower edge by the moulding to the upper edge, at which the second enclosure commenced, was two cubits high. This height is reckoned from the upper edge of the חיק, or from the first (lowest) ledge. The height of these three portions taken together, therefore, was (1 + 2 + 4) seven cubits. To this the mount of God (<hi type="italic">s</hi>), which was four cubits (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.15">Eze 43:15</reference>), has to be added, making in all eleven cubits. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.14">Eze 43:14</reference> חיק is followed by הארץ: the חיק consisting of earth, or filled with earth. But the חיק, with its moulding, is designated גּב, the back or support of the altar, and is thereby distinguished from the altar itself; so that, for the height of the altar, we have only to reckon the two enclosures, with the mount of God, which amount to ten cubits. Upon the basis of the חיק, with its moulding, and the two enclosures (עזרה), there rose the true altar, with its hearth, and the horns at the four corners, noticed in Eze 43:15. A distinction is here made between הראל, i.e., mount of God, and אריאל; and they are not to be identified, as they have been by many of the commentators, down to Hitzig, after the example of the lxx. אריאל (as the word is to be written according to the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>) does not mean “lion of God,” but “heart of God” (ארי, from ארה, to burn), as in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">Isa 29:1</reference>-2.
